4.1.11 Displacement of Ukrainian nationals continues, particularly from occupied and conflict-affected areas, with the International Organization for Migration (IOM) estimating that 58% of internally displaced persons (approximately 2.25 million people) originated from raions under full or partial occupation. The largest concentrations of internally displaced persons are located in Dnipropetrovska oblast (611,000), Kharkivska oblast (469,000), Kyiv city (341,000) and Kyivska oblast (315,000). As of September 2025, IOM estimated that there were approximately 4.5 million returnees who had previously been displaced residing in government-controlled areas of Ukraine (see Displacement).

4.1.12 Between 1 January 2025 and 30 June 2026, the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) recorded 123,424 security incidents across Ukraine, including battles between armed forces, explosions and remote violence and incidents of violence against civilians. The number of recorded security incidents increased from 37,571 during the first half of 2025 to 45,182 during the first half of 2026. ACLED also recorded 109,155 conflict-related fatalities, including both civilians and military service personnel, during the same period (see Origins of the invasion and events, Displacement, Military casualties and Fatalities and injuries).

4.1.13 Conflict-related violence continues to result in civilian injuries and fatalities across Ukraine. The United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) verified 2,514 civilian fatalities and 12,142 civilian injuries during 2025, compared with 2,088 civilian fatalities and 9,138 civilian injuries during 2024. During the first 6 months of 2026, HRMMU verified a further 1,396 civilian fatalities and 7,978 civilian injuries, compared with 1,122 civilian fatalities and 5,734 civilian injuries during the corresponding period in 2025 (see Civilian injuries and fatalities). HRMMU noted that these figures are likely to underestimate the true number of civilian casualties, as only verified cases are included. However, when considered against Ukraine’s estimated population of approximately 39.5 million people (see Population), the overall number of verified civilian casualties remains low. The 14,656 civilian casualties verified during 2025 represented approximately 0.04% of the population (see Civilian injuries and fatalities).

4.1.14 Data published by ACLED indicates significant geographical variation in the scale and intensity of violence. Of the 123,424 security incidents recorded between 1 January 2025 and 30 June 2026, approximately 83% occurred in Donetsk, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts. Donetsk alone accounted for 35,367 incidents, whilst Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts each recorded more than 14,000 incidents. By contrast, western oblasts including Chernivtsi, Zakarpattia, Ternopil, Volyn and Ivano-Frankivsk each recorded fewer than 100 incidents during the same period (see Number and locations of security events).

4.1.15 ACLED fatality data indicates a similar pattern. Of the 109,155 conflict-related fatalities (military personnel and civilians) recorded between 1 January 2025 and 30 June 2026, 45,943 occurred in Donetsk oblast and 42,362 occurred in Kherson oblast – therefore accounting for approximately 81% of all recorded fatalities. Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk and Sumy oblasts also recorded higher numbers of combined military and civilian fatalities than much of the remainder of Ukraine (see Number and locations of security events).

4.1.16 Civilian casualties, including both injuries and fatalities, are recorded across a wider geographical area than active conflict events and conflict-related fatalities. HRMMU reported that 63% of the 14,656 civilian casualties verified during 2025 occurred in frontline areas. During the first 7 months of 2026, civilian casualties were recorded in between 12 and 20 regions each month. Between January and June 2026, HRMMU verified 9,374 civilian casualties, of which approximately 35% to 45% resulted from long-range missile and drone attacks. Such attacks caused deaths and injuries in urban areas located more than 30 kilometres from the frontline. However, the greatest concentration of civilian harm remained in Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. Whilst Kyiv also records relatively high numbers of civilian casualties as a result of long-range attacks, the available information does not indicate that casualties occurred at such a frequency or scale that a civilian would, solely on account of their presence in the city, face a real risk of serious harm (see Civilian injuries and fatalities).

4.1.17 However, decision makers must consider each case on its facts. Even where there is not a real risk of serious harm by reason of indiscriminate violence in a situation of armed conflict in general, a person may still face a real risk of serious harm if they are able to show that there are specific reasons over and above simply being a civilian affected by indiscriminate violence.

4.1.18 For guidance on considering serious harm where there is a situation of indiscriminate violence in an armed conflict, including consideration of enhanced risk factors, see the Asylum Instruction, Humanitarian Protection.

5. Protection

5.1.1 The state is generally not able to provide protection against a breach of Article 3 ECHR because of indiscriminate violence in a situation of armed conflict if this occurs in individual cases.

5.1.2 For further guidance on assessing state protection, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

6. Internal relocation

Version 3.0, October 2026

Executive summary

Ukraine continues to be affected by an international armed conflict following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. Russian forces continue to occupy parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts, as well as Crimea.

The situation remains fluid as the conflict is ongoing. Decision makers should consult sources and tools such as ACLED’s Ukraine Conflict Monitor for ongoing and near real-time information when considering cases.A state of war, civil instability and/or where law and order has broken down do not of themselves establish a well-founded fear of persecution for a Refugee Convention reason. As such, the question is whether the person faces a real risk of serious harm such that they qualify for Humanitarian Protection.

In general, in Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Sumy and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, particularly in frontline, near-frontline and border areas, the level of indiscriminate violence is at such a high level that there are substantial grounds for believing that a civilian would, solely on account of their presence in those oblasts, face a real risk of serious harm within the meaning of paragraphs 339C and 339CA(iv) of the Immigration Rules.

Active hostilities are concentrated in the eastern, southeastern and northeastern parts of the country, particularly in frontline and border areas. As such, the level of indiscriminate violence throughout the rest of Ukraine is not at such a high level that that test is met. This includes:

(a) in areas where Ukrainian forces are not directly engaging with the Russian military, or facing frequent missile attacks; and

(b) oblasts away from the frontline which may have also experienced violence and civilian casualties, often because of increased Russian long-range missile and drone strikes.

The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise. Decision makers must consider each case on its facts.

The state is generally not able to provide protection against serious harm arising from indiscriminate violence in a situation of armed conflict.

Internal relocation is likely to be reasonable in general. There are parts of Ukraine where the level of indiscriminate violence does not reach the threshold required to establish a real risk of serious harm solely on account of a person’s presence there, including areas outside the frontline, near frontline and border regions most affected by the conflict.

Ukraine is a designated state under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002. However, due to the ongoing conflict, where a claim is refused it is unlikely to be certifiable as clearly unfounded.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts. The onus is on the person to demonstrate they face persecution or serious harm.

Assessment

Section updated: 31 August 2026

About the assessment

This section considers relevant evidence – including country information, refugee and human rights law and policy, and case law – to assess whether, in general:

the security situation is such that there are substantial grounds for believing there is a real risk of serious harm because there exists a serious and individual threat to a civilian’s life or person by reason of indiscriminate violence in a situation of international or internal armed conflict as within paragraphs 339C and 339CA(iv) of the Immigration Rules

the state (or quasi state bodies) can provide effective protection

internal relocation is possible to avoid persecution or serious harm

if refused, a claim is likely or not to be certified as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents country information, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes.

1. Material facts, credibility and other checks

1.1.1 Decision makers must:

assess credibility (see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status).

check if there has been a previous application for a UK visa or another form of leave. Asylum applications matched to visas should be investigated prior to the asylum interview (see the Asylum Instruction on Visa Matches, Asylum Claims from UK Visa Applicants).

consider making an international biometric data-sharing check, when one has not already been undertaken (see Biometric data-sharing process (Migration 5 biometric data-sharing process)).

consider language analysis testing, where available, in cases where there are doubts surrounding a person’s claimed place of origin (see the Asylum Instruction on Language Analysis).

Official – sensitive: Not for disclosure – Start of section

The information in this section has been removed as it is restricted for internal Home Office use.

Official – sensitive: Not for disclosure – End of section

2. Exclusion

2.1.1 Decision makers must consider whether there are serious reasons to apply one (or more) of the exclusion clauses. Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

2.1.2 If the person is excluded from the Refugee Convention, they will also be excluded from a grant of humanitarian protection, which has a wider range of exclusions than refugee status.

2.1.3 For guidance on exclusion and restricted leave, see the Asylum Instruction on Exclusion under Articles 1F and 33(2) of the Refugee Convention, Humanitarian Protection and the instruction on Restricted Leave.

13.2.31 In relation to the presence of mines and other explosive ordnance, the same source stated: ‘The risk posed by mines and other explosive ordnance remained consistently high during April– June 2026, with no evidence of a meaningful reduction across assessed frontline, near-frontline and previously conflict-affected areas. The highest levels of risk continued to be reported in Kherson, Mykolaiv, Kharkiv and Donetsk Oblasts, where longstanding contamination is compounded by ongoing hostilities, repeated shelling, remote mining and the expanding use of FPV drones. Although no confirmed mine or UXO incidents were identified through protection monitoring in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia Oblasts during the reporting period, explosive ordnance remained a significant concern due to repeated strikes and the potential presence of unexploded munitions following attacks.’[footnote 61]

14. Freedom of movement

14.1.1 Article 33 of the Constitution of Ukraine guarantees freedom of movement, choice of residence and the right to leave the territory of Ukraine[footnote 62]. See Country Policy and Information Note, Ukraine: Military Service for information on how martial law affects freedom of movement.

14.1.2 In their 2026 annual report, Freedom House noted that:

‘The full-scale invasion has caused significant displacement. … the danger of land mines and unexploded ordnance prevents refugees and IDPs from returning home …

‘… Mobilization reforms of 2024 obligated all men of military age to self-report their updated location, biographic data, and contact information in a new government-run mobile application. …

‘In August 2025, the Ukraine government announced that men aged 18 to 22 would be permitted to cross the country’s borders freely. Previously, men aged 18 to 60 were barred under martial law from leaving the country. The Ukrainian government framed the policy change as an effort to help young Ukrainians maintain ties with the homeland and pursue education abroad, while also responding to demographic pressures and youth discontent.’[footnote 63]

14.1.3 In July 2026, the UNHCR published Ukraine Protection Survey 3 based on a survey of households across government-held Ukraine. The survey examined a range of protection issues safety and freedom of movement. The UNHCR stated that the survey:

‘… provides analysis of over 13,000 interviews conducted in three intervals within a year from April 2025 to April 2026 … Qualitative information of 476 key informant interviews conducted in 51 hromadas during the three survey rounds complements the quantitative analysis. Data collection took place from March to April 2025 (Protection Survey 1), August to September 2025 (Protection Survey 2) and from March to April 2026 (Protection Survey 3).’[footnote 64]

14.1.4 The Ukraine Protection Survey 3 noted that:

‘80% of respondents can enjoy their freedom of movement in Ukraine (areas under temporary occupation are excluded), while 17% report some limitations to their freedom of movement. Compared to the first survey round a year ago, a slight deterioration in people’s ability to move freely by 3% was

observed in the second and third round. Male respondents report higher limitations to their freedom of movement at 21% compared to female (14%), further elevated to 25% among younger male respondents with an average age of 44 years. War-affected respondents also report higher barriers

to their freedom of movement than IDPs and returnees at 25%.

‘Respondents with specific needs exhibit more movement limitations at 22%, further heightened to over 25% if respondents are above 60 years. Specifically, older persons at risk and single-headed household stand out as the two categories with greatest movement restrictions at 28% and 32%.’[footnote 65]

14.1.5 The same survey looked at respondents’ reported reasons constraining freedom of movement:

‘Risk of air raid sirens and air attack is a main reason constraining people’s freedom of movement (35%). Returnees (52%) and war-affected (45%) respondents report this constraint more often than IDPs (30%). Female respondents also report these concerns more often (46%) than males (41%), while it is a lesser concern among older respondents (31%) than

younger ones (38%).

‘13% of respondents note constraints due to the lack of barrier-free infrastructure or transport as well as lack of assistive devices. These constraints are highest among respondents over 60 years at 19% as well as those with specific needs at 21%. This constraint is also heightened for IDPs at 16% compared to war-affected (10%) and returnee (10%) respondents.

‘Overall, 21% of respondents do not have their own transport and 8% cannot afford public transport. IDPs report more

often than others not having their own transport at 22%, while affordability constraints for public transport remain at 8%.

This constraint is reportedly also higher among female respondents with 23% reporting not having their own transport,

and 10% facing affordability constraints (as compared to 19% and 5% respectively among males).

‘23% report limitations to their freedom of movement due to mobilization risks, and 11% due to the checkpoints. Both are

significantly elevated for male respondents at 41% and 20% respectively, and are the top two constraining factors for

males of younger age.
